¶
'''blandisher''' (blan′dish-ėr), ''n.'' One who blandishes; a flatterer.

'''blandishing''' (blan′dish-ing), ''n.'' [< ME. ''blandisinge''; verbal n. of ''blandish.''] Blandishment.
{{smaller block|<poem>Double-hearted friends, whose ''blandishings''
Tickle our ears, but sting our bosoms.</poem>
{{right|''J. Beaumont'', Psyche, vi. 3.}}}}

'''blandishing''' (blan′dish-ing), ''a.'' [< ME. ''blaundyshing''; ppr. of ''blandish.''] Mild; soothing.
{{smaller block|The see hath eke his ryght to be somtime calm and ''blaundyshing'' with smothe water.
{{right|''Chaucer'', Boëthius, ii., prose 2.}}}}

'''blandishment''' (blan′dish-ment), ''n.'' [< OF. ''blandissement'', < ''blandir'': see ''blandish'' and ''-ment.''] '''1.''' Speech or action expressive of affection or kindness, and tending to win the heart; an artful caress; flattering attention; cajolery; endearment.
{{smaller block|<poem>As thus he spake, each bird and beast behold
Approaching two and two; these cowering low
With ''blandishment'': each bird stoop’d on his wing.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., viii. 351.}}
''Blandishments'' will not fascinate us.
{{right|''D. Webster'', Speech, Bunker Hill.}}}}
'''2.''' Something bland or pleasing; that which pleases or allures.
{{smaller block|The rose yields her sweete ''blandishment.''
{{right|''Habington'', Castara, ii.}}}}
readings.c1s3:
¶
{{smaller block|The ''blandishments'' of early friendships.
{{right|''Longfellow'', Hyperion, iv. 5.}}}}

'''blandly''' (bland′li), ''adv.'' In a bland manner; with suavity; mildly; gently.

'''blandness''' (bland′nes), ''n.'' [< ''bland'' + ''-ness.''] The state or quality of being bland; mildness; gentleness; soothingness.
{{smaller block|Envy was disarmed by the ''blandness'' of Albemarle’s temper.
{{right|''Macaulay'', Hist. Eng., xxiii.}}}}

'''blandurilla''' (blan-dū-ril′ä̤), ''n.'' [Sp., dim. of ''blandura'', softness, a white paint used by women, < ''blando'', soft, bland, < L. ''blandus'': see ''bland''<sup>2</sup>, ''a.''] A fine soft pomatum made in Spain.

'''blank''' (blangk), ''a.'' and ''n.'' [Early mod. E. also ''blanc'', ''blanck''; < ME. ''blank'', fem. ''blanche'' (see ''blanch''<sup>1</sup>, ''a.''), < OF. ''blanc'', fem. ''blanche'', white (= Pr. ''blanc'' = Sp. ''blanco'' = Pg. ''branco'' = It. ''bianco''; ML. ''blancus''), < OHG. ''blanch'', MHG. ''blanc'', G. ''blank'', shining, bright (= MLG. ''blank'' = D. ''blank'' = Sw. Dan. ''blank'', shining, = AS. *''blanc'', only in poet. deriv. ''blanca'', a white or gray horse, ME. ''blanke'', ''blonke'', Sc. ''blonk''; cf. Icel. ''blakkr'', poet., a horse, steed); usually referred to a Teut. verb *''blinkan'' (pret. *''blank''), shine, which, however, is not found in the older tongues: see ''blink''. In the sense of a coin (II., 7, 8), OF. ''blanc'', MLG. ''blank'', MD. ''blancke'' (ML. ''blanca''), orig. with ref. to the color of silver.] '''I.''' ''a.'' '''1.''' White or pale: as, “the ''blanc'' moon,” ''Milton'', P. L., x. 656.
{{smaller block|''Blank'' as death in marble.{{right|''Tennyson'', Princess, i.}}}}
'''2.''' Pale from fear or terror; hence, dispirited; dejected; confounded; confused.

'''II.''' ''n.'' '''1.''' Any void space or vacant surface; a space from which something is absent or omitted; a void; a vacancy: as, a ''blank'' in one’s memory; to leave ''blanks'' in writing.
{{smaller block|I cannot write a paper full as I used to do, and yet I will not forgive a ''blank'' of half an inch from you. ''Swift.''
<poem>From the cheerful ways of men
Cut off, and for the book of knowledge fair
Presented with a universal ''blank''
Of nature’s works, to me expunged and rased.</poem>
{{right|''Milton'', P. L., iii. 48.}}}}
'''2.''' A piece of paper prepared for some special use, but without writing or printed matter on it.
{{smaller block|The freemen signified their approbation by an inscribed vote, and their dissent by a ''blank.'' ''Palfrey.''}}
'''3.''' A form or document containing blank spaces; a document remaining incomplete till something essential is filled in.
{{smaller block|<poem>And daily new exactions are devis’d—
As ''blanks'', benevolences, and I wot not what.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Rich. II., ii. 1.}}}}
'''4.''' In parliamentary usage, provisional words printed in italics in a bill, the final form of which is to be settled in committee.—'''5.''' A ticket in a lottery on which no prize is indicated; a lot by which nothing is gained.
{{smaller block|In a lottery where there are (at the lowest computation) ten thousand ''blanks'' to a prize, it is the most prudent choice not to venture.
{{right|''Lady M. W. Montagu'', Letters, Jan. 28, 1753.}}}}
'''6.''' In ''archery'', the white mark in the center of

a butt or target at which an arrow is aimed; hence (archaically), the object toward which anything is directed; aim; target.
{{smaller block|As level as the cannon to his ''blank.''
{{right|''Shak.'', Hamlet, iv. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Let me still remain
The true ''blank'' of thine eye.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', Lear, i. 1.}}}}
{{smaller block|<poem>Quite beyond my arm, out of the ''blank''
And level of my brain.</poem>
{{right|''Shak.'', W. T., ii. 3.}}}}
'''7.''' Same as ''blanc'', 1.—'''8.''' A small copper coin formerly current in France.
{{smaller block|Refuse not a marvedi, a ''blank.''
{{right|''Middleton and Rowley'', Spanish Gypsy, ii. 1.}}}}
'''9.''' A piece of metal prepared to be formed into some finished object by a further operation: as, a ''blank'' for a file or a screw; specifically, in coining, a plate or piece of gold or silver, cut and shaped, but not stamped.—'''10.''' A blank verse.
{{smaller block|<poem>Five lines of that number,
Such pretty, begging ''blanks.''</poem>
{{right|''Beau. and Fl.'', Philaster, ii. 2.}}}}
'''11†.''' A weight, equal to <math>\tfrac{1}{230400}</math> of a grain.

'''blank''' (blangk), ''v. t.'' [< ''blank'', ''a.''] '''1†.''' To make blank; make white or pale; blanch.
{{smaller block|Blount arose and left the hall, while Raleigh looked after him with an expression that ''blanked'' for a moment his bold and animated countenance.
{{right|''Scott'', Kenilworth, I. xvii.}}}}

A coarse woolen fabric, white or undyed, used for clothing.—'''2.''' A large oblong piece of soft, loosely woven woolen cloth, used for the sake of its warmth as a bed-covering, or (usually made of coarser material and closer texture) as a covering for a horse when standing or exposed to cold, and sometimes worn as a garment, especially among rude or uncivilized people.—'''3.'''
